extracted.intended_audience: architects, preservationists, and public custodians of monuments (Victorian-era/academic readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles for designing, teaching, selecting styles, and conserving architecture so that buildings retain character, age-worthiness, and national unity of form. Emphasizes maintenance over restoration, obedience to established laws/styles, appropriate choice of materials, and pedagogy for architects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picturesque must not destroy original character
rubrics_metrics.description: The superinduced and accidental beauty is most commonly inconsistent with the preservation of original character; the picturesque is therefore sought in ruin, and supposed to consist in decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the picturesque is merely extraneous (rents, fractures, stains, vegetation) it assimilates architecture with nature and may be loved; but when such extraneous beauty extinguishes true architectural characters, it is merely picturesque and harmful. The artist who values ivy over the pillar shaft is abandoning essential character for surface effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for the building's aged appearance (age-worthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A building cannot be considered as in its prime until four or five centuries have passed over it; the entire choice and arrangement of its details should have reference to their appearance after that period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None should be admitted which would suffer material injury by weather-staining or mechanical degradation over such a lapse; the external signs of age are 'exponents of age' and may be ranked among pure and essential characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration is effectively destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither by the public, nor by those who have the care of public monuments, is the true meaning of the word restoration understood. It means the most total destruction which a building can suffer: a destruction out of which no remnants can be gathered; a destruction accompanied with false description of the thing destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to restore lost finish is conjectural; direct copying of worn surfaces is impossible and results in cold, hard imitation. The usual process of 'restoration' is to dash old work to pieces and put up cheap basest imitation; if restoration is necessary, accept it as destruction and act honestly (pull down, reuse materials), but do not erect false substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer continuous maintenance to later restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Take proper care of your monuments, and you will not need to restore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive measures (a few sheets of lead on the roof, sweeping leaves from water-courses) will save roof and walls. Watch an old building with anxious care; guard it continually; bind with iron where it loosens; stay with timber where it declines. Better a crutch than a lost limb; do this tenderly, reverently, and continually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings are communal heritage—do not alter them for present convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no right whatever to touch them. They belong partly to those who built them, and partly to all the generations of mankind who are to follow us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What men of past generations intended to be permanent must not be obliterated for present convenience. The right over such works does not pass with death; we must not cast down buildings for present ease; destruction imposes sorrow and loss upon millions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose wanton or ignorant destruction (mob/committee-driven)
rubrics_metrics.description: The people who destroy anything causelessly are a mob, and Architecture is always destroyed causelessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Destruction by mobs, by deliberate folly, or even by committees is illegitimate; no cause now is valid to destroy fine buildings (criticizes modern neglect then restoration to create work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose style according to materials and their durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Those styles of architecture whose decoration depends on the arrangement of points of shade rather than on purity of outline do not suffer, but commonly gain in richness of effect when their details are partly worn away; hence such styles...should always be adopted when the materials to be employed are liable to degradation...and styles dependent on purity of line...must be practised altogether in hard and undecomposing materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: French Gothic suits soft materials (brick, sandstone, soft limestone); Italian (pure-line) Gothic requires granite, serpentine, or crystalline marbles. The nature of accessible materials influenced formation of styles and should determine choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture must be subject to universal law and school
rubrics_metrics.description: The architecture of a nation is great only when it is as universal and as established as its language; and when provincial differences of style are nothing more than so many dialects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No individual caprice should materially vary accepted types and customary decorations; from cottage to palace every member of architecture should be as commonly current as language or coin. A national, accepted code (school) is necessary for greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience, not unbounded liberty, is the crowning principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Obedience is...the crowning grace of all the rest...Obedience is, indeed, founded on a kind of freedom, else it would become mere subjugation, but that freedom is only granted that obedience may be more perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraint (law) produces fairness and perfection; too much restraint is harmful, but balance between inherent character and superior law yields beauty. Architecture requires stricter laws than other arts because of its social scale and permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not seek novelty or new style for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: We want no new style of architecture...It is of marvellously little importance whether [our laws] be new or old...But it is of considerable importance that we should have a code of laws of one kind or another, and that code accepted and enforced from one side of the island to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality in expression does not depend on inventing new forms; a gifted man will work in the style of his day and make it fresh. Striving for novelty by rebelling against common laws will harm the art; better to master an accepted style first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogy: enforce strict copyism and grammatical mastery first
rubrics_metrics.description: When we begin to teach children writing, we force them to absolute copyism...So, when a boy is first taught to write Latin, an authority is required of him for every expression he uses...In the same way our architects would have to be taught to write the accepted style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by determining authoritative 'Augustan' buildings, study modes of construction and laws of proportion penetratingly, catalogue forms and decorations; admit not so much as an alteration in the depth of a cavetto or breadth of a fillet until mastery. Only after habitual fluency should license be permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit limited license only after mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Then, when our sight is once accustomed to the grammatical forms and arrangements...then, and not till then, a license might be permitted; and individual authority allowed to change or to add to the received forms, always within certain limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorations may be variable and enriched with original ideas, but changes should be natural, instructive and within controlled limits—like liberties a great speaker takes with language, not defiance of rules for singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select historically substantial styles; avoid infantile or barbarous vulgarizations
rubrics_metrics.description: We are equally precluded from adopting styles essentially infantine or barbarous, however Herculean their infancy, or majestic their outlawry, such as our own Norman, or the Lombard Romanesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice should consider adaptability to modern uses and popular sympathy; the vulgarization of Greek architecture is condemned, and late flamboyant extremes are unsuitable because their grammatical laws are hard to limit. The choice between classical and Gothic must weigh practical adaptation and popular regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should lead other arts via enforced common practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture must be the beginning of arts, and that the others must follow her in their time and order...the prosperity of our schools of painting and sculpture...depends upon that of our architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a universally adopted system of form and workmanship, other arts will languish; this requires consent of architects and the public to choose and use a style universally, even if achieving that consent seems impossible.
